# Equipment Lending Club Database

## Original brief

Design a database for a small equipment-lending club, operated by one librarian on a single offline workstation. Use three entities: members (id, full_name, unique email), items (id, unique asset_tag, name), and loans (id, member_id, item_id, borrowed_on, nullable returned_on). A member and an item each have many historical loans; every loan has one member and one item. No payments, bookings, authentication tables or locations. Store UTC dates. Keep loan history and RESTRICT deletion of referenced members/items. Require returned_on >= borrowed_on when present. Use SQLite. Seed at least three realistic rows per table with returned and open loans. The app, not a SQL CHECK, ensures at most one open loan per item. A library clerk is the only trusted user; protect the local file using OS permissions and backups. This is a wholly synthetic public test, not the course scenario.md.

## Initial understanding

A single-user offline SQLite database for a small equipment-lending club managed by one librarian. It tracks members (with unique email), items (with unique asset_tag), and loans (with borrowed_on and nullable returned_on UTC timestamps). Loan history is retained with RESTRICT deletion on referenced members and items. The application enforces at most one open loan per item; returned_on must be >= borrowed_on when present.

## Actors

- Library clerk (librarian)

## Candidate entities

- members (id, full_name, unique email)
- items (id, unique asset_tag, name)
- loans (id, member_id, item_id, borrowed_on, nullable returned_on)

## Main processes

- Borrowing an item (create a loan record)
- Returning an item (set returned_on)
- Viewing loan history for members and items
- Adding or editing members and items

## Questions and risks

- The 'at most one open loan per item' rule is enforced by the application, not the database, so a bug could create duplicate open loans.
- The returned_on >= borrowed_on requirement may be enforced by the application or a CHECK constraint; this is ambiguous.
- Single offline workstation creates a single point of failure; backup strategy is mentioned but not detailed.
- No authentication table; access control relies entirely on OS file permissions.
- Email and asset_tag uniqueness are enforced at the DB level but there is no verification that emails are valid or owned.
- RESTRICT deletion means loans cannot be deleted, which preserves history but may complicate corrections.

conceptual-model.md.content:
# Conceptual model — Equipment Lending Club Database

**Design version:** 3 · **Target:** SQLite

A single-user offline SQLite database for a small equipment-lending club. It tracks members with unique email and optional phone, items with unique asset tags, and loans with borrow/return dates. The schema enforces unique constraints, RESTRICT deletion on referenced members/items, and a CHECK constraint that returned_on is not before borrowed_on. The application ensures at most one open loan per item within a transaction. Security relies on OS file permissions and regular backups.

## Entities

### members

Club members with unique email and optional phone

### items

Lendable equipment items with unique asset tag

### loans

Loan records linking a member and an item with borrow and return dates

## Entity-relationship diagram

```mermaid
erDiagram
  members {
    integer id PK
    text full_name
    string email
    string phone
  }
  items {
    integer id PK
    string asset_tag
    text name
  }
  loans {
    integer id PK
    integer member_id FK
    integer item_id FK
    date borrowed_on
    date returned_on
  }
  members ||--o{ loans : "member_id"
  items ||--o{ loans : "item_id"
```

## Relationships and cardinality

- loans (member_id) → members (id): many-to-one; required parent; parent deletion: RESTRICT. A parent can have zero or many matching child records.
- loans (item_id) → items (id): many-to-one; required parent; parent deletion: RESTRICT. A parent can have zero or many matching child records.

## Business rules

- At most one open loan per item: enforced by the application within a transaction (not by a SQL constraint).
- returned_on must be >= borrowed_on when present: enforced by the SQL CHECK constraint loans_return_check.
- Email must be unique: enforced by the UNIQUE constraint on members.email.
- Asset tag must be unique: enforced by the UNIQUE constraint on items.asset_tag.
- Deletion of a member or item that has existing loans is restricted: enforced by ON DELETE RESTRICT on foreign keys.
- Loan history is retained indefinitely; no cascading deletes.
- All foreign keys (member_id, item_id) are mandatory and must reference existing rows.

| member_id | INTEGER | No | — | Foreign key to members.id |

| returned_on | DATE | Yes | — | UTC date (YYYY-MM-DD) when the item was returned, null if still out |

# Normalization analysis

**Design version:** 3 · **Target:** SQLite

## Method

1NF requires atomic attributes and unique rows. 2NF excludes partial dependencies on part of a composite candidate key. 3NF excludes non-key transitive dependencies. Surrogate primary keys alone do not prove 3NF. The following dependency claims must be reviewed against the actual business semantics.

## members

### Functional dependencies

- id -> full_name, email, phone
- email -> id, full_name, phone

### Normal-form assessment

The table is in 3NF: all non-key attributes depend on the primary key id, and email is a candidate key with no transitive dependencies; phone is also functionally dependent on id.

## items

### Functional dependencies

- id -> asset_tag, name
- asset_tag -> id, name

### Normal-form assessment

In 3NF: all attributes depend on the primary key, and asset_tag is a candidate key with no transitive dependencies.

## loans

### Functional dependencies

- id -> member_id, item_id, borrowed_on, returned_on

### Normal-form assessment

In 3NF: all attributes depend on the primary key; no transitive dependencies; foreign keys are required.

## Deliberate denormalization

No deliberate denormalization. Every table is intended to satisfy at least 3NF.

## Validation boundary

Execution checks prove syntax and constraint/seed compatibility, not the truth of functional dependencies. A human must confirm semantic normalization.

# Assumptions and remaining ambiguity

**Design version:** 3 · **Target:** SQLite

- No limit on the number of open loans a member can have simultaneously.
- The application enforces at most one open loan per item inside a transaction; the database does not have a constraint for this rule.
- Email addresses are not format-validated by the database; the database enforces uniqueness, while format validation is an application responsibility.
- Asset tags are unique but not verified to be physically attached to items.
- Backup strategy is not detailed; regular file-based backups are assumed.
- Database file access is controlled entirely by OS permissions; no additional encryption or authentication table is used.
- borrowed_on and returned_on are date-only UTC values stored as YYYY-MM-DD strings (review correction).
- IDs are integers assigned by the application; the database does not use auto-increment.
- Members may have an optional phone number; if provided, it is stored as a string of up to 30 characters.

## Operational assumptions

- Run schema.sql in an existing empty database with appropriate CREATE privileges. Do not run it against production.
- Seed data is synthetic and contains no real personal information.
- Sample data is not an exhaustive performance or security test.
- Monetary decimal values are illustrative; production applications should use exact decimal serialization.
- All generated files derive from one canonical design model, included as design.json in the export.
- The design is model-generated and needs human domain review before production use.

schema.sql.name: schema.sql
schema.sql.content:
-- Equipment Lending Club Database
-- Target: SQLite. Run in a new, empty database.
-- IDs are explicitly supplied by the application; no identity/sequence allocation is assumed.

PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;

CREATE TABLE "members" (
  "id" INTEGER NOT NULL,
  "full_name" TEXT NOT NULL,
  "email" VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  "phone" VARCHAR(30),
  PRIMARY KEY ("id"),
  UNIQUE ("email"),
  CHECK (length("email") <= 255),
  CHECK (length("phone") <= 30)
);

CREATE TABLE "items" (
  "id" INTEGER NOT NULL,
  "asset_tag" VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  "name" TEXT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY ("id"),
  UNIQUE ("asset_tag"),
  CHECK (length("asset_tag") <= 50)
);

CREATE TABLE "loans" (
  "id" INTEGER NOT NULL,
  "member_id" INTEGER NOT NULL,
  "item_id" INTEGER NOT NULL,
  "borrowed_on" DATE NOT NULL,
  "returned_on" DATE,
  PRIMARY KEY ("id"),
  CONSTRAINT "loans_return_check" CHECK (returned_on IS NULL OR returned_on >= borrowed_on),
  FOREIGN KEY ("member_id") REFERENCES "members" ("id") ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  FOREIGN KEY ("item_id") REFERENCES "items" ("id") ON DELETE RESTRICT
);

CREATE INDEX "loans_item_returned_idx" ON "loans" ("item_id", "returned_on");

CREATE INDEX "loans_member_idx" ON "loans" ("member_id");

intake.title: Equipment Lending Club Database
intake.summary: A single-user offline SQLite database for a small equipment-lending club managed by one librarian. It tracks members (with unique email), items (with unique asset_tag), and loans (with borrowed_on and nullable returned_on UTC timestamps). Loan history is retained with RESTRICT deletion on referenced members and items. The application enforces at most one open loan per item; returned_on must be >= borrowed_on when present.
entities: loans (id, member_id, item_id, borrowed_on, nullable returned_on)
processes: Borrowing an item (create a loan record)
Viewing loan history for members and items
Adding or editing members and items
risks: The 'at most one open loan per item' rule is enforced by the application, not the database, so a bug could create duplicate open loans.
The returned_on >= borrowed_on requirement may be enforced by the application or a CHECK constraint; this is ambiguous.
Single offline workstation creates a single point of failure; backup strategy is mentioned but not detailed.
No authentication table; access control relies entirely on OS file permissions.
Email and asset_tag uniqueness are enforced at the DB level but there is no verification that emails are valid or owned.
RESTRICT deletion means loans cannot be deleted, which preserves history but may complicate corrections.

choice.rationale: SQLite remains the optimal choice because the system is a single-user offline application; the review corrections (date-only fields, clarified email handling) do not change the deployment model or requirements, and SQLite's CHECK constraints, UNIQUE enforcement, and RESTRICT foreign keys fully support the design.

comparison.strengths: Zero-configuration serverless architecture, direct local file access, lightweight, supports CHECK constraints and RESTRICT foreign keys, easy file-based backups.
comparison.tradeoffs: Lacks multi-user concurrent writes, but the application serializes writes and runs on a single offline workstation anyway.
comparison.verdict: Selected. Explicitly requested and ideally suited for a single-user, offline, low-complexity local deployment.

comparison.strengths: Robust open-source engine, excellent SQL standard support, strong data integrity and concurrency features.
comparison.tradeoffs: Requires running a background server, client-server configuration, and ongoing administrative overhead for a single-user app.
comparison.verdict: Rejected. Over-engineered for a simple single-user desktop app; introduces unnecessary server and operational complexity.

comparison.strengths: Popular relational database with good performance and standard client-server capabilities.
comparison.tradeoffs: Requires a running server daemon and client-server networking, adding unnecessary deployment overhead for a local tool.
comparison.verdict: Rejected. Server-based architecture is unnecessary and adds complexity for a single-user offline application.

comparison.strengths: Enterprise-grade features, robust engine, and powerful official management tooling.
comparison.tradeoffs: Heavy licensing costs, large resource footprint, and complex installation for a simple local database.

design.name: Equipment Lending Club Database
design.overview: A single-user offline SQLite database for a small equipment-lending club. It tracks members with unique email and optional phone, items with unique asset tags, and loans with borrow/return dates. The schema enforces unique constraints, RESTRICT deletion on referenced members/items, and a CHECK constraint that returned_on is not before borrowed_on. The application ensures at most one open loan per item within a transaction. Security relies on OS file permissions and regular backups.

columns.name: phone
columns.description: Optional phone number, private contact data

tables.normalization: The table is in 3NF: all non-key attributes depend on the primary key id, and email is a candidate key with no transitive dependencies; phone is also functionally dependent on id.

columns.name: id
columns.description: Unique loan identifier assigned by the application

columns.name: borrowed_on
columns.description: UTC date (YYYY-MM-DD) when the item was borrowed

columns.name: returned_on
columns.description: UTC date (YYYY-MM-DD) when the item was returned, null if still out

checks.name: loans_return_check
checks.expression: returned_on IS NULL OR returned_on >= borrowed_on

tables.normalization: In 3NF: all attributes depend on the primary key; no transitive dependencies; foreign keys are required.

assumptions: No limit on the number of open loans a member can have simultaneously.
The application enforces at most one open loan per item inside a transaction; the database does not have a constraint for this rule.
Email addresses are not format-validated by the database; the database enforces uniqueness, while format validation is an application responsibility.
Asset tags are unique but not verified to be physically attached to items.
Backup strategy is not detailed; regular file-based backups are assumed.
Database file access is controlled entirely by OS permissions; no additional encryption or authentication table is used.
borrowed_on and returned_on are date-only UTC values stored as YYYY-MM-DD strings (review correction).
IDs are integers assigned by the application; the database does not use auto-increment.
Members may have an optional phone number; if provided, it is stored as a string of up to 30 characters.
businessRules: At most one open loan per item: enforced by the application within a transaction (not by a SQL constraint).
returned_on must be >= borrowed_on when present: enforced by the SQL CHECK constraint loans_return_check.
Email must be unique: enforced by the UNIQUE constraint on members.email.
Asset tag must be unique: enforced by the UNIQUE constraint on items.asset_tag.
Deletion of a member or item that has existing loans is restricted: enforced by ON DELETE RESTRICT on foreign keys.
Loan history is retained indefinitely; no cascading deletes.
All foreign keys (member_id, item_id) are mandatory and must reference existing rows.
security: The SQLite database file is protected by operating system file permissions (e.g., read/write for the librarian only).
Regular backups of the database file should be maintained to prevent data loss.
Emails and phone numbers are private contact data; consider encrypting the database file if required by policy.
No authentication table; access is via the application which is used solely by the trusted librarian.
